title: Days of the Week: An Album a Day
subtitle: Featuring Deftones, Bill Evans, Nicki Minaj, and others
contentHtml:
My friend Ken and I decided to listen to an album every day this year. Each week is themed. At the end of each week, we rank what we listened to. To be clear, we aren’t ranking every album that fits the theme. We are only ranking what we chose to listen to during the last seven days.

This week’s theme is “days of the week,” meaning the album title had to contain the name of the day of the week we were listening. This was a much trickier than anticipated. There are lots of Friday and Saturday album titles. There aren’t many Tuesdays or Wednesdays.

#7 Wednesday by Chris Webby (2017)

The first track on Chris Webby’s Wednesday is a time capsule. “Fuck Donald, fuck Ivanka,” the Connecticut rapper begins, before laying into Rex Tillerson, Jeff Sessions, Kid Rock, Scott Pruitt, Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio, Ben Carson, Mike Pence, and basically everybody else in the orbit of the first Trump administration. (He also dishes some insults at Bill and Hillary Clinton before declaring, “Long live Bernie.”)

Independent of your political leanings, the first thing that crossed my mind while listening to this political diss track was, “Wow! It’s been a long decade.” The second thing that crossed my mind was, “Wow! This song is horrendous.” One bad song isn’t a problem. The problem is that the rest of the album isn’t any better.

Chris Webby sounds like what I imagine Eminem sounds like to people who hate Eminem. His rhymes are filled with unmemorable insults. His beats sound like they came preloaded on a Casio keyboard you got in middle school. And his raspy tone resembles someone just trying to figure out how to rap. The only joy I got out of listening to Wednesday was finding out that Ken opened for Chris Webby at some point.

#6 Thursday by The Weeknd (2011)

During 21st century covers week, I reviewed Echoes of Silenceby The Weeknd. Here’s what I wrote about it:

The Weeknd is a rare pop star in that he arrived more or less fully-formed. Before he’d even dropped a single, the Canadian singer put out a trio of albums (or mixtapes) in a year. The last of those albums was Echoes of Silence. It’s got everything you’d come to hear on his biggest hits.

You’ve got the sensual R&B (e.g., “Montreal”). You’ve got the beats that make you feel like you’re in a haunted house (e.g., “XO / The Host”). And, of course, you’ve got the crisp upper vocal register seamlessly shifting between falsetto and head voice (e.g., “Next”). If you want The Weeknd without any of the baggage that comes with the hits you’ve heard 1,000 times, this is a great place to turn.

Thursday is another of those “trio of albums (or mixtapes)” that The Weeknd dropped before his debut studio album. And it left the exact same impression on me as Echoes of Silence did. Given that, why is Thursday near the bottom of the rankings when Echoes of Silence was in the middle of the pack?

Ken hated it, almost irrationally. “Maybe my limit for The Weeknd is one album per year,” he theorized. I think he was just probably in a bad mood. One thing I’ve learned this year is that your mood impacts how an album hits you.

#5 Pink Friday by Nicki Minaj (2010)

Like The Weeknd, Nicki Minaj built her resume with many releases before her proper debut record. Yes, both released mixtapes in their pre-album era, but unlike The Weeknd, Minaj’s reputation grew most from her features. Her work on Young Money’s “BedRock,” Ludacris’s “My Chick Bad,” and Trey Songz’s “Bottoms Up” made her feel like a hit-song Swiss Army knife. Soon after, she hopped on Kanye West’s “Monster.” The new kid on the block was now rapping circles around legends, and she ackowledged as much:

So let me get this straight, wait, I’m the rookie?
But my features and my shows ten times your pay?
50K for a verse, no album out

“Monster” is in the middle of Kanye West’s magnum opus, My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy. It’s a sinister posse cut where West is joined by Jay-Z, Rick Ross, and Minaj. And the greenhorn pulls out all her tricks. The alter egos. The crazed rhymes. The off-kilter flows. Her dynamism makes Jay-Z look like Chris Webby.

One month later, Minaj’s debut album Pink Friday finally came out—coincidentally on the same day as My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy. And it’s got all of those same tricks that Minaj broke out on “Monster.” The only difference is that there are more pop-oriented songs. In fact, Nicki Minaj sings a bunch of the hooks (e.g., “Save Me”). These don’t hit as hard as the rap-focused tracks. Better to have Natasha Bedingfield or Rihanna handle the hook if you’ve got the option. But when she trades the melodies for rhymes, you can tell why everyone wanted her on their songs at the time.

Even so, my main thought while listening to this record was that I often prefer a Nicki Minaj feature to a full Nicki Minaj song. Of course, she can carry an entire track. But I find her more compelling when she just appears for a verse or two.

#4 No Fun Mondays by Billie Joe Armstrong (2020)

Last month while writing his survey of COVID-era music, Steven Hyden described how most of it has been memory holed. “The challenge of writing about the lockdown era is that nobody remembers it,” he noted. “Not that nobody wants to remember it. Or that it’s not worth remembering. We have just collectively decided, as a society, to wipe it from our memory banks.” Hyden then goes on to recount some things that have been completely forgotten despite somewhat warm receptions at the time, like Post Malone and Travis Barker doing an 80-minute Nirvana tribute. No Fun Mondays is another of these COVID-forgotten memories.

“No Fun Mondays” began as a series where Billie Joe Armstrong would post a cover to Green Day’s YouTube channel each Monday. After doing 14, Armstrong packaged them up and put them together as an album bearing the name of the series.

Nothing on No Fun Mondays is groundbreaking. This is not Jimi Hendrix doing “All Along the Watchtower.” Some songs make complete sense, like “Kids in America.” Others work surprisingly well, like “Manic Monday.” And others miss the mark, like John Lennon’s “Gimme the Truth.”

I’m sure in the doldrums of COVID-19’s first summer, this was all very entertaining. In fact, I kind of remember being into Armstrong’s version of “I Think We’re Alone Now.” But I don’t think it had anything to do with that particular cover. I just love that song. No song could save me from my COVID malaise, though. Not even “I Think We’re Alone Now.” There is no need to think of aloneness when you are deep inside it.

#3 Saturday Night Wrist by Deftones (2006)

TikTok has reinvigorated interest in many older bands and songs over the last decade. “Put Your Head on My Shoulder” by Paul Anka (1959). “Pretty Little Baby” by Connie Francis (1962). “Dreams” by Fleetwood Mac (1977). Every old song or artist that goes viral on the short-form video app has left me with some level of surprise. Why that particular song and not the other older work I’ve deemed a masterpiece? But I don’t think any surprise has left me more gobsmacked than that of Deftones.

Deftones are ostensibly a metal band that launched in 1988. But they aren’t metal in the same sense that Metallica and Megadeth are metal. They, despite the riffs, bear more resemblance to Faith No More and Nine Inch Nails than any of the thrash gods. This is metal that’s willing to find influence in more unexpected places. (On their 2011 covers album, they reinterpret songs by Jawbox, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Duran Duran, and The Cars.) It is alternative in all broad senses of the word.

So, what has Gen Z found in Deftones’ strain of alternative metal that has made the Sacramento group more popular than ever before? Sure, some of it is the power of the riffs you hear on “Hole in the Earth” or the screams on “Rats!Rats!Rats!”. But I think it mostly comes down to the horny moodiness.

As discussed extensively in Liz Pelly’s Mood Machine and more briefly in Chapter 13 of my book, much listening on streaming services is driven by vibe. You want the music you play while cooking or studying to feel a certain way. Many Deftones songs, especially those on Saturday Night Wrist, happen to have this moodiness that many rock bands and rappers have tapped into over the last 15 years (e.g., “Cherry Waves”).

On top of that, there is a sexuality—sometimes explicit (e.g., “Pink Cellphone”) often implicit—that plays very well on social media. Search their name on TikTok and find scores of women strutting and posing to their songs. In other words, a decades-old band happens to be perfectly situated for the current moment. They’ve got the riffs. They’ve got the energy. They’ve the vibes. And they’ve got the sex. Any other artist that could simultaneously tap into all of this would surely be a millionaire.

#2 Tuesday Night Music Club by Sheryl Crow (1993)

Though I don’t think it is as consistently strong as her self-titled record we listened to earlier this year, Tuesday Night Music Club has some real highs. “Strong Enough” is a complex yet powerful love song. The stream of consciousness narration in “All I Wanna Do” is pure fun. And “I Shall Believe” is the perfect closer to burn off the album.

But there are misses. “Leaving Las Vegas,” a small hit upon release, is packed with cliche imagery of Sin City (e.g., “And I check the odds / And I, and I place my bet / I pour a drink”). “The Na-Na Song” sounds like a cheap knockoff of Bob Dylan’s “Subterranean Homesick Blues.” Tuesday Night Music Club is, in a word, uneven.

Sheryl Crow has a magic trick, though. She’s got an incredible voice. She can handle a pop song but the subtle rasp in her voice evokes blues singers of yore. And with that voice, Crow can still dazzle even if her material falls short.

#1 Sunday at the Village Vanguard by Bill Evans Trio (1961)

Unlike God on the seventh day, Bill Evans and his trio did not rest on Sunday. They were hard at work at the Village Vanguard, the Greenwich Village club primarily known for its jazz. And though they worked hard, what they performed is the perfect music for a day of rest.

These recordings are subdued but alive, the trio of instruments weaving between one another with grace. They are not easy recordings. There is depth to what the Bill Evans Trio is doing. But I can’t imagine a better album to throw on while loafing about on a Sunday.

Murdered Musicians: An Album a Day

This week’s theme is “murdered musicians,” meaning albums by artists who were killed by someone else. We’ve had some grim themes this year (e.g., swan songs), but this is the most macabre by far. Luckily, the albums themselves were not as grisly.

Butt Rock: An Album a Day

This week’s theme is “butt rock,” meaning post-grunge from the late 1990s or early 2000s. “Butt rock,” of course, is a derisive moniker. The term allegedly emerged from radio stations whose slogan was some variant of “Nothing but rock.” Haters then added a “t” and ran with it. But Ken and I are not going in with a bad attitude. Are we listening to nothing but rock this week? Yes. But we’ll only double that last “t” when it’s actually necessary.
